newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: EARLY OUTLOOK FOR S.AFRICAN 1997 MAIZE CROP GOOD.
newsitem.headline: EARLY OUTLOOK FOR S.AFRICAN 1997 MAIZE CROP GOOD.

text.p: South Africa's National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said on Wednesday conditions looked favourable for the 1997 crop which farmers were in the early stages of planting.
"At this stage conditions are looking very good," Nampo economist Andre Ferreira told Reuters.
Ferreira said long-term weather forecasts indicated that the industry could expect a good crop.
"If you couple this to good moisture status then it seems as if we can expect a reasonably good crop," Ferreira said.
He said farmers in Mpumulanga province had completed planting while in the Free State they had only just began.
Farmers in the NorthWest province had not yet started to plant for the new season, he added.
Last season, some 3.3 million hectares were planted from which the National Crop Estimates Committee said it expected a harvest of 9.48 million tonnes, up from the 4.41 million in the previous year.
Nampo warned South African farmers last month only to plant on their best land to prevent a surplus in the coming season.
On Wednesday the producers reiterated the warning.
"Ideally we should have about three million hectares planted under maize. Last year a little bit more than 3.3 million hectares was planted," Nampo general manager Giep van Zyl said.
"In effect there are 300,000 to 400,000 hectares too much. This could only lead to bigger surpluses," he added.
Asked what the maize crop would be if farmers heeded Nampo's warning, van Zyl said: "About 7,5 to 8 million tonnes of maize.
"Our warning to the producer is do not plant to try and produce surpluses for exports because the world price of maize is falling.
"We are also saying farmers should only plant on their best land, where they are certain to make a profit even at a lower price," he added.
The Maize Advisory Committee said last month that discussions on future maize marketing arrangements for next season would be discussed at its meeting on November 22.
In September, South Africa's parliament passed the Marketing of Agricultural Products Bill which sets a 13-month timetable for the dismantling of remaining farming control boards .
The bill also compels industries to manage their affairs on a market-related basis.
